opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few conditions, and they often come together.

The first is control over your data. Many enterprises, especially in regulated industries like finance, healthcare, or government, are very uncomfortable sending sensitive data outside their perimeter. If you can run a model in your own VPC or on-prem, that concern largely goes away. Open models make that much easier.

The second is customization. The frontier proprietary models are very good general-purpose models, but most enterprise applications aren't general-purpose. They're narrow: classifying support tickets, extracting fields from documents, answering questions over internal knowledge. For these tasks, you can often take a smaller open model, fine-tune it on your own data, and get quality that matches or even beats a much larger proprietary model. And once you've done that, the model itself becomes part of your intellectual property, a differentiator rather than something every competitor can also call through the same API.

The third is cost and performance at scale. When you're prototyping, calling an API is the fastest way to go, and I think most companies should start there. But once an application is in production at high volume, the economics change. A smaller, specialized model can be an order of magnitude cheaper to serve, with lower latency, and you control the hardware and the serving stack, so you can optimize for your workload.

The fourth is predictability. With a hosted model, the provider can update or deprecate it, and suddenly your carefully tuned prompts behave differently. With an open model, you pin the version and it behaves the same tomorrow as it does today. For enterprises, that stability matters a lot.

So the pattern I expect is something like this: start with proprietary models to figure out whether the application is valuable at all. Then, as it matures and you understand the task, move toward open models that you can specialize, own, and run cheaply. In practice, most enterprises will end up with a mix, using the frontier proprietary models for the hardest, most open-ended reasoning and open models for the large volume of more well-defined tasks.

The last point is the gap between them. As long as open models stay reasonably close in quality, which has largely been the trend, I think these other factors, meaning control, cost, and customization, will increasingly tip the balance toward open source for a lot of enterprise workloads.

r001.rationale: The response says enterprises value control over sensitive data, deployment in their own VPC or on-prem, and pinning model versions.

r002.rationale: It says enterprises can use smaller open models when they match or beat proprietary models on narrow enterprise tasks, and need only remain reasonably close in quality for enterprise workloads.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to start with what we've actually seen. If you look at the history of software, open source eventually dominates in almost every layer of the stack — operating systems, databases, web servers, big data, you name it. Linux, Postgres, Spark, Kubernetes. It took time, but it happened. And the reason is pretty simple: once the technology stabilizes enough that it becomes a commodity, the advantages of open source — control, cost, no lock-in, the ability to customize — start to outweigh whatever edge the proprietary offering has.

So the question for AI models is really: when does the gap between the best proprietary model and the best open model become small enough that it doesn't matter for a given use case? And I think we're already there for a lot of enterprise workloads. If you look at the leaderboards — and we run Chatbot Arena, so we see this very directly — the gap between the frontier closed models and the best open models like Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen has been shrinking. It used to be a year, now it's months, and for many tasks the difference is basically noise.

But there are a few specific conditions that push enterprises toward open models. The first one is data. Enterprises have proprietary data, it's their crown jewels, and many of them simply cannot or do not want to send it to a third-party API — whether that's regulatory, like healthcare or finance, or just competitive. With an open model you run it in your own VPC, on your own infrastructure, and the data never leaves.

The second one is customization. For most enterprise applications you don't need the smartest general-purpose model in the world. You need a model that's very good at your task — your documents, your customer support tickets, your code base. And when you fine-tune an open model on your data, a 7B or 70B model can often match or beat a frontier model on that narrow task, at a fraction of the cost and latency. You can't do that kind of deep customization with a closed model, or at least not in the same way.

The third is economics. Once you're running at scale, inference cost dominates. Per-token API pricing looks great when you're prototyping and terrible when you have millions of users. If you own the model and the serving stack — and this is a lot of what we've worked on with vLLM — you control that cost curve, and you can optimize it.

And then the fourth, which I think people underestimate, is predictability and control. With an API, the provider can change the model, deprecate it, change the pricing, change the terms. Your application behavior can shift overnight. For an enterprise that's building something they need to maintain for five or ten years, that's a real risk. An open model that you've pinned, evaluated, and deployed is a stable foundation.

Now, where will proprietary models still win? At the frontier. If you need the absolute best reasoning, the newest capabilities, the latest multimodal stuff, the closed providers will probably stay a few months ahead for a while. And for companies that don't have the engineering talent to run their own infrastructure, the convenience of an API is worth a lot. Not everyone wants to be in the business of operating GPUs.

So my view is it's going to look like most other layers of the stack. Proprietary at the very edge, for the most demanding or novel use cases, and open models for the bulk of production workloads — especially as the tooling around them, the serving, fine-tuning, evaluation, gets more mature. And honestly, I think that transition is happening faster than almost anyone expected a couple of years ago.

r001.rationale: The candidate says open models offer enterprises control over data, infrastructure, costs, and model stability, and that these advantages can outweigh a proprietary model’s edge.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the proprietary–open model gap need only be small enough for a given use case, and that open models can match or beat frontier models on specific enterprise tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think enterprises will prefer open-source models when those models are good enough for their application and give them more control over cost, data, and deployment. You don’t necessarily need the best model in the world for every task. You need a model that meets your quality requirements at a cost you can afford.

For example, if you have sensitive data and you want to run the model inside your own infrastructure, open source can be very attractive. Or if you have a specialized application, you may be able to customize a smaller model and get very good performance at a much lower cost, particularly at high volume.

But there is a tradeoff. Running and maintaining a model requires expertise. If you don’t have that expertise, or a proprietary model gives you substantially better results, using an API may make more sense. So I expect enterprises to use a mix, choosing based on the requirements of each application.

r001.rationale: The response says enterprises may prefer open-source models when they provide more control over cost, data, and deployment, while meeting application needs.

r002.rationale: The response says models need to be good enough for the application and meet its quality requirements, adding that enterprises do not need the best model for every task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on the application. If an open-source model gives you the quality you need, then cost, control, and privacy become very important. An enterprise may want to keep its data in its own environment, customize the model, and avoid depending on a single provider. Those are strong reasons to use open source.

But you have to look at the total cost. Running a model yourself requires infrastructure and expertise. For some companies, using an API will be much simpler and cheaper. And if a proprietary model is significantly better on a task that matters to your business, you may be willing to pay for that.

So I expect enterprises to use a mix. The question is whether an open model is good enough for a particular workload, and whether the benefits of controlling it outweigh the operational costs.

r001.rationale: The response identifies control as a strong reason to use open source and says enterprises weigh control’s benefits against operating costs, conveying a preference for greater control when other factors are comparable.

r002.rationale: It says an open model needs to provide the quality needed for a particular workload, while enterprises may pay for a proprietary model that is significantly better on a task that matters to them.
